citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., and Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI.
creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Microsoft Research AI, Carnegie Mellon University, University of Washington)
description: PIQA is a benchmark dataset for physical commonsense reasoning in natural language. It consists of multiple-choice questions where a model must choose the most sensible solution to a physical goal from two options. The dataset contains over 16,000 training QA pairs with additional development and test sets, inspired by instructables.com and designed to test knowledge of physical properties, affordances, and object manipulation.
name: PIQA (Physical Interaction: Question Answering)
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each item was validated by multiple annotators; examples with low inter-annotator agreement were removed. Human performance was calculated by majority vote among annotators who achieved 90% on the qualification HIT.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotators were Amazon Mechanical Turk workers who passed a qualification HIT with >80% accuracy. Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr according to self-reporting on turkerview.com and internal timing calculations. No further demographic information (nationality, age, gender, etc.) is provided.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human performance on the development set was measured at 94.9% accuracy via majority vote among qualified annotators (those achieving 90% on the qualification HIT). Examples with low annotator agreement were removed during validation, often filtering out items requiring expert-level domain knowledge. Annotator pay was verified at >$15/hr via self-reporting on turkerview.com and internal timing calculations.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon Mechanical Turk (HITs — Human Intelligence Tasks)
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were shown an instructable page as inspiration and asked to provide: (1) a physical goal, (2) a valid solution, and (3) a "trick" — a subtly incorrect solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. A qualification HIT was run first requiring >80% accuracy on well-formed and underspecified (goal, solution) pairs. Data was collected in batches and validated by other annotators for correctness; users with low agreement were de-qualified. A diff button was provided in the interface to highlight differences between solutions. During validation, examples with low agreement were removed. Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr.
rai:dataBiases: Reporting bias was identified as a major concern: when thinking about how to achieve a goal, people are drawn to prototypical solutions and common tools (e.g., kitchen utensils, garage tools), rarely considering the hundreds of other everyday objects. To address this, annotators were prompted with instructables links to encourage atypical solutions and flatten the distribution of referenced objects. Annotation artifacts (stylistic biases that artificially inflate model performance) were removed using the AFLite algorithm. The dataset was specifically constructed to be adversarial to BERT to avoid trivial solutions exploiting surface-level patterns.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected via crowdsourcing using Amazon Mechanical Turk (HITs). Annotators were prompted with links to instructables.com pages (covering six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop) and asked to construct goal-solution pairs. Each annotator provided: (1) a physical goal, (2) a valid solution, and (3) a "trick" — a subtly incorrect solution that sounds plausible. Two examples were drawn per instructable. Annotators were pre-qualified via a qualification HIT requiring >80% accuracy. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators. AFLite was then applied to remove annotation artifacts.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Instructables.com pages served as the seed/inspiration for annotations. Instructables is a crowdsourced collection of instructions for activities ranging from cooking to car repair, often including images or videos detailing each step and a list of required tools.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, User-generated content data
rai:dataLimitations: Examples requiring expert-level domain knowledge (e.g., special woodworking terminology) were removed during validation as they fall outside the scope of "commonsense." Some model "mistakes" on the development set were found to actually be correct answers that required a web search to verify. The dataset focuses on physical commonsense expressible in language, and does not cover physical knowledge that can only be acquired through direct physical interaction with the world.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: AFLite algorithm was applied to remove annotation artifacts and spurious biases. AFLite fine-tunes BERT-Large on 5,000 examples to compute embeddings of all remaining instances, then uses an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets to identify instances whose embeddings are highly indicative of the correct answer label. Such instances are discarded. Goals were tokenized using Spacy; solutions were tokenized using the GPT BPE tokenizer for analysis. Examples were truncated at 150 tokens for model experiments (affecting ~1% of data).
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance AI systems' understanding of physical commonsense, which is critical for building language models useful beyond NLP — particularly for robotics and embodied agents that interact with the physical world. The authors argue that knowledge should ultimately be learned from interaction with the world rather than language alone, and PIQA is intended to highlight this gap and motivate future research.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding models. Probing the physical knowledge encoded in large pretrained language models. Studying the gap between language-based AI and human physical understanding. Advancing language representations that capture physical world knowledge for applications in robotics and embodied AI.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: AFLite algorithm using BERT-Large for computing embeddings to detect and remove annotation artifacts. Spacy tokenizer used for tokenizing goals. GPT BPE tokenizer used for tokenizing solutions during analysis.
